writer: Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5), agent mode: claims written from the tree, statistics and engine facts, then machine-checked

intro.text: The Berlin Defence is Black's most solid answer to the Ruy Lopez. In this course White meets it with a calm protecting pawn move instead of the heavily analysed endgame lines.

You will learn the main line where White exchanges bishop for knight to give Black doubled pawns, the solid setups Black often chooses instead, and four common club mistakes with the exact way to punish each one.
Every line ends when the engine agrees the position is resolved: either one side is clearly better or the position is equal and both plans are clear.

claims.text: White occupies the centre with a pawn and opens lines for the queen and the light-squared bishop.
Black takes an equal share of the centre. Both sides now want to develop quickly and fight for the central squares.
The knight develops towards the centre and attacks Black's centre pawn, so Black must spend the next move defending it.
The most natural defence: Black protects the pawn with a developing move.
The Spanish bishop attacks the knight that defends Black's centre pawn. It does not win that pawn yet, but it creates long-term pressure on Black's centre that lasts well into the middlegame.

principle.text: Development with pressure: every White move in the Ruy Lopez either develops a piece or adds pressure on Black's centre.

claims.text: Instead of first asking the bishop what it wants, Black develops the other knight and counterattacks White's centre pawn at once.
Most club players now castle, which allows the sharp lines where Black takes the pawn; this course uses a calmer setup.

White simply protects the centre pawn with another pawn. There is no need to learn the long forcing lines after castling, and the pieces stay on the board for a manoeuvring game where plans matter more than memory.
In 1600–2200 club games it scores about 56% for White, as well as castling does.
In the main line White develops with Nbd2 and castles before starting any action.

principle.text: Solid centre first, active pieces second: once the centre is safe White can choose between pressure on Black's pawn and a later central break.

claims.text: Black puts the bishop on its most active diagonal, aimed at White's kingside. This is the most common reply at every level.
It is the most frequent reply in our club sample.
White gives up the bishop for the knight on purpose. The knight was Black's best defender of the centre pawn, and the trade forces Black to accept doubled pawns.

principle.text: Trading a bishop for a knight is fine when it damages the opponent's pawns or removes a key defender; here it does both.

claims.text: Black recaptures with the d-pawn. That opens the d-file and frees the light-squared bishop, which is why this is the standard recapture.
Black now has doubled c-pawns and the bishop pair, and the d-file is half-open for Black.
The queen's knight develops behind the pawns. It does not block the c-pawn's path forever: it is heading for a better square on the queenside or kingside.
In the main line White castles and then jumps to Nc4, where the knight eyes Black's centre pawn and the queenside.
Black reroutes the knight so that the f-pawn can support the centre and the knight can come to a more useful square later.
Black typically castles and then supports the centre with the f-pawn.
White completes development and gets the king safe. The middlegame plans start from here.
White's queenside plan: knight to c4, then c3 and b4 to gain space and push Black's bishop back.
Both sides have castled. Black has the two bishops; White has the better pawn structure and will try to gain space before Black's bishops become active.
From here the knight pressures Black's centre pawn and supports a queenside advance.
The next step is to gain queenside space with the c- and b-pawns.
Black supports the centre pawn with the f-pawn. The structure is now very solid, but the light squares around Black's king are a little weaker.
Black delays the knight manoeuvre and castles. White's reply is the same idea: bring the knight to its good square.
White continues with Nc4 and castles.
Black develops the light-squared bishop and keeps the option of castling queenside. White calmly castles and keeps the knight flexible.

e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 d3 Bc5 Bxc6 dxc6 N.title: Castle and keep the knight flexible

claims.text: With Black's bishop covering the knight's favourite square, White looks for another route for the knight or a queenside expansion with the b-pawn.
Black prevents White's queenside expansion by fixing the a-pawn first. White's knight still goes to its best square.
Black secures the bishop's retreat in advance. White reacts in the centre instead of on the queenside.
Black protects the centre pawn with a pawn and keeps a closed, solid position. This is the second most common reply.
About a quarter of club players choose it.
White castles first. In closed positions it pays to finish development before committing the pawns.
The rook comes to the e-file next to support a later central break.
Black breaks the pin on the knight in advance so that the bishop-for-knight exchange no longer damages the pawns.
Black pins the knight to the queen and adds pressure on White's centre. White answers in the centre rather than chasing the bishop at once.
White prepares and then plays d4 to gain the centre.
Black asks the bishop to decide. White exchanges it, giving Black doubled pawns before Black can drive it away.
White exchanges with check before Black can drive the bishop back, so Black has to accept damaged pawns.
Black has doubled c-pawns, a lasting target for White's pieces.
A modest but sound developing move. White builds the classical Spanish pawn centre.
White prepares the central advance with c3 and the rook on the e-file.
Black re-routes the knight towards the kingside so that the c-pawn can support a later central advance. White simply develops.
The bishop defends the centre pawn but blocks Black's d-pawn and the queen's line. White develops normally and can later exchange the bishop for the knight to double Black's pawns.
Asking the bishop sounds natural, but here it loses time: White exchanges the bishop for the knight and then takes Black's undefended centre pawn.
White removes the knight that guards Black's centre pawn. After the recapture that pawn is weak.
Black recaptures away from the centre. The centre pawn has lost its defender.
White wins a clean pawn with a good position: this is why the bishop exchange came first.

whitePlan.text: White is a clean pawn up. Finish development with O-O and Re1, then open the centre with d4 while Black is still undeveloped.

blackPlan.text: Black is a pawn down without real compensation. The practical try is fast development and activity for the two bishops.

claims.text: A typical club move that keeps White's pieces off a kingside square but ignores the centre. White exchanges the bishop for the knight and wins Black's centre pawn.
Same theme as the other quiet mistakes: once the defender is gone, the centre pawn falls.

whitePlan.text: Block the check with c3, castle, then Re1 and d4: the extra pawn and the better structure decide.

blackPlan.text: Black is a pawn down and should aim for active piece play rather than passive defence.

claims.text: The bishop is passive here and, more importantly, the centre pawn still depends only on the knight. White exchanges the bishop for the knight and takes it.
Black moves the same knight twice and offers a trade that helps White. After the exchange White gains time with a central pawn advance.
Black's recapturing pawn now stands far forward, and Black's remaining knight can be chased.
With the bishop already prepared to retreat, White takes the centre. Black's pin on the knight is annoying but not dangerous.
Black asks the bishop to decide; White prefers the exchange that damages Black's pawns.
Exchanging with check gives Black doubled pawns before the bishop can be trapped or forced back.
Black now has doubled c-pawns.
Black recaptures towards the centre, keeping more pawns there.
White asks the pinning bishop to decide: take on the knight, or retreat and keep the pin.
Black keeps the pin. The bishop is active, but it can later become a target for White's kingside pawns.
The rook protects White's centre pawn so that Black's pieces cannot win it.
Black regroups the knight and prepares to release the central tension.
White develops the last knight and keeps the centre protected.
Black exchanges in the centre so that White's centre pawn becomes a target.
White recaptures towards the centre and now has two central pawns side by side.
The queen attacks Black's weakened queenside pawns and stops the black queen from coming out easily.
Black gets rid of the weak pawn by advancing it and challenging White's centre.
White opens lines towards Black's uncastled king and the remaining weak pawns.
The pawn capture comes with tempo against Black's bishop, so Black must recapture at once.
White gains queenside space and keeps Black's knight out of its best square.
Black uses the moment to break in the centre and activate the pieces.
White's queen takes the central pawn; the open position now favours White's more active pieces slightly.
The queen protects Black's centre pawn and prepares to castle queenside or connect the rooks.
With the bishop covering the knight's usual square, White prepares to develop the dark-squared bishop on the long diagonal.
The bishop goes to Bb2 next.
Black uses the a-pawn to gain space and to annoy White's queenside.
The bishop aims at Black's centre pawn and prepares a central break.
Black adds a defender to the centre pawn and keeps the position compact.
The knight attacks Black's light-squared bishop to win the bishop pair back or to force a concession.
Black protects the centre pawn with the bishop, which also prevents White from simply capturing it.
The knight eyes the queenside squares and prepares a central break.
White pins the knight to the queen and prepares the central break.
With pieces in place, White opens the centre to use the better pawn structure.
The knight reaches its ideal square at once, where it pressures Black's centre pawn.
Black protects the centre pawn and prepares to support it with the f-pawn.
White castles and keeps all options in the centre and on the queenside.
The pawn stops Black from chasing the knight away with the b-pawn.
White offers to trade Black's active dark-squared bishop.
The knight goes to its best square anyway; Black's a-pawn did not prevent this.
Black supports the centre pawn with the f-pawn, the standard setup in this structure.
White prepares the central break and gives the queen a route to the queenside.
Black gains space and drives White's knight away from its good square.
The knight retreats towards the kingside, where it eyes a strong square in front of Black's king.
White opens the centre now that Black's queenside pawns have advanced and left weaknesses.
White removes the knight that guards Black's centre pawn.
After the recapture Black's centre pawn has no defender.
The recapture away from the centre leaves Black's centre pawn undefended.
White collects the pawn. Black's bishops give some activity, but White is simply a pawn up.
White prepares the central break and gives the bishop a retreat square.
Black finishes development and waits to see White's plan.
The rook supports White's centre pawn before the central break.
Black asks the bishop to retreat; in this structure White prefers to keep it.
White keeps the light-squared bishop, which later returns to the long diagonal aiming at Black's king.
Prepares the queenside pawn advance and keeps Black's pieces out of White's half of the board.
The point is b4 next, gaining space with tempo against the bishop.
Black protects the centre pawn once more and makes room for the dark-squared bishop to drop back.
The bishop will retreat to Bf8 when attacked.
The pawn advance gains queenside space and forces Black's bishop to give up its active diagonal.
The bishop retreats to defend the kingside. Black is solid but a little passive.
White develops the last minor piece and contests the dark squares Black's bishop used to control.
Next comes a4 to add more queenside space.
Black develops with Be6 first and brings the knight back to Nd7 later with better timing.
White's queenside pawns now restrict Black's queenside pieces.
White connects the rooks with Qc2 and regroups with Nfd2.
Black finally develops the light-squared bishop and challenges White's well-placed knight.
The queen connects the rooks and stays useful on both wings.
Black's queen supports the bishop and prepares a queenside reaction.
The knight steps back so that White's f-pawn can join the fight later.
White prepares the f-pawn break with f3 and later f4.
Black's knight returns to its best regrouping square. Both sides are fully developed and the position is balanced.

claims.text: Protecting the centre pawn with a pawn avoids the queen trade and long forcing lines of the main Berlin. The game stays rich: White plays slowly, improves the pieces and chooses the moment to strike in the centre or on the queenside.

glossary.title: Doubled c-pawns for the bishop pair

claims.text: When the bishop takes the knight and Black recaptures towards the centre, Black gets two bishops and an open file but a damaged queenside. White's long-term trump is the healthy kingside pawn majority, which can later create a passed pawn, especially in an endgame.

In these closed Spanish structures the queen's knight rarely stays on its first square. It develops behind the pawns and then goes to the queenside to support an advance, or to the kingside to support an attack.
